```{r}
# Re-run the field-minus-molecular increment under each treatment of the queue.
incr <- function(model_file, N = 2000, seed = 7) {
  source(here::here("R", model_file), chdir = TRUE)   # each redefines des_run() cleanly
  arm <- function(s) des_run(modifyList(inputs, list(strategy = s, N = N)), seed = seed) |>
    group_by(name) |> summarise(c = sum(dcost), q = sum(dqaly), .groups = "drop") |>
    summarise(c = mean(c), q = mean(q))
  m <- arm("mol"); f <- arm("field")
  c(dcost = f$c - m$c, dqaly = f$q - m$q)
}
drift <- rbind(
  `8  — no queue`           = incr("model-8.R"),
  `9  — exogenous wait`     = incr("model-9.R"),
  `10 — endogenous (A)`     = incr("model10.R"),
  `11 — endogenous (B)`     = incr("model11.R"))
quad <- ifelse(drift[,"dcost"] < 0 & drift[,"dqaly"] > 0, "SE (dominant)",
        ifelse(drift[,"dcost"] < 0 & drift[,"dqaly"] < 0, "SW (cheaper, worse)", "other"))
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(`Δ cost` = round(drift[,"dcost"]), `Δ QALY` = round(drift[,"dqaly"], 3),
             Quadrant = quad, check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "The same field-vs-molecular decision, under four treatments of the confirmatory queue.")
```

Read the `Δ QALY` column top to bottom: **+0.26 → +0.27 → −0.02 → −0.02**. The cost column
never changes sign — the field test is cheaper in every row, because its cost advantage is
the *test*, and the queue does not touch that. What the queue moves is the **health** axis,
and it moves it across zero. Ignoring capacity, or modelling it exogenously, the field test
is **dominant** (southeast): an easy yes. Model the bottleneck *endogenously* — by either
design — and the same field test lands in the **southwest**: still cheaper, but now *worse*
for health, because the referrals it generates overwhelm the confirmatory capacity and its
extra cancers progress untreated in the line. The recommendation does not merely weaken; it
**flips quadrant**. A decision-maker who saw only Models 8–9 would adopt the field test as a
free win. A decision-maker who saw Models 10–11 faces a genuine trade-off: real savings
bought with real health loss — the "southwest-quadrant quandary."

## How much capacity? A sensitivity sweep

The flip from SE to SW is not a knife-edge — it is a smooth function of how many confirmation
slots the system has. We sweep the capacity from generous to severe, for *both* designs,
averaging several independent cohorts at each level (the incremental QALY is small near the
boundary, so a single cohort is noisy).

```{r}
#| label: capacity-sweep
cap_incr <- function(model_file, cap, seeds, N = 2000) {
  source(here::here("R", model_file), chdir = TRUE)   # silent (sys.nframe guard); defines des_run
  arm <- function(strat, seed)
    des_run(modifyList(inputs, list(strategy = strat, N = N, cap.confirm.per1000 = cap)), seed = seed) |>
      group_by(name) |> summarise(c = sum(dcost), q = sum(dqaly), .groups = "drop") |>
      summarise(c = mean(c), q = mean(q))
  d <- vapply(seeds, function(s) { m <- arm("mol", s); f <- arm("field", s); c(f$c - m$c, f$q - m$q) },
              numeric(2))
  c(dcost = mean(d[1, ]), dqaly = mean(d[2, ]))
}
seeds <- c(7, 101, 202, 303) * 1009L   # widely spaced -> independent cohorts (avoid bank overlap)
caps  <- c(12, 6, 3, 2)                # confirmation slots per 1,000 eligible people
A <- t(vapply(caps, function(k) cap_incr("model10.R", k, seeds), numeric(2)))
B <- t(vapply(caps, function(k) cap_incr("model11.R", k, seeds), numeric(2)))
verdict <- function(dc, dq) ifelse(dc < 0 & dq > 0, "SE — adopt",
                            ifelse(dc < 0 & dq < 0, "SW — reject", "—"))
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    `Slots/1,000` = caps,
    `Δcost (A)` = round(A[,"dcost"]), `ΔQALY (A)` = round(A[,"dqaly"], 3), `(A)` = verdict(A[,"dcost"], A[,"dqaly"]),
    `Δcost (B)` = round(B[,"dcost"]), `ΔQALY (B)` = round(B[,"dqaly"], 3), `(B)` = verdict(B[,"dcost"], B[,"dqaly"]),
    check.names = FALSE),
  align = "rrrlrrl",
  caption = "Field vs molecular by confirmatory capacity — Approach A and B side by side (4 independent cohorts averaged, N = 2000). Both flip SE → SW between 6 and 3 slots per 1,000.")
```

Read down either `ΔQALY` column: the field test's health advantage shrinks as slots are removed
and **crosses zero between 6 and 3 slots per 1,000** — for *both* designs. Above that the
bottleneck has slack and the field test is dominant (adopt); below it the referral flood
saturates the queue and the field test is dominated on value (reject at the \$100k threshold).
Cost is negative at every level — capacity moves only the health axis. Two readings matter:

- **The lever is capacity, as a number.** The recommendation is not "field test: yes or no" but
  "field test **and** confirmatory capacity above roughly six slots per 1,000." Adopt the cheap
  test *without* expanding the bottleneck and the program lands in the southwest.
- **A and B agree across the whole range.** Averaged over cohorts, the two designs track each
  other to within a few hundredths of a QALY at every capacity — and give the *same*
  recommendation at every row. The convenient analytic wait (A) is an entirely adequate
  stand-in for the exact queue (B) for this mean-CEA question; B is reserved for questions about
  the wait *distribution* rather than its average.


## Approach A vs B: where they agree, and where they part

The capacity sweep already gave the headline answer: averaged over cohorts, the two designs
land in the same quadrant at every capacity and track each other to within a few hundredths
of a QALY. But that sweep paired the two *strategies* within each model (common random
numbers) and then compared the two models' *means*. We cross-check it with a fully
independent estimator, because there is a subtlety worth stating: **CRN can align two
strategies inside one model, but not two different models.** A and B inject different
confirm-handling events into the loop, so the reactive resample consumes each patient's
disease bank at a different cadence; a shared-seed A-vs-B comparison measures that cadence
artifact, not the models (we even see A ≠ B under a null-effect run, where the queue is
inert). So the head-to-head must be done by independent replication.

::: {.callout-note}
## A = B on the bottom line (30 independent replications)
Over 30 independent cohorts with CRN disabled (`validation/validate-AB-replication.R`), A and
B **agree on both axes** within Monte-Carlo error: the field test is cheaper by ≈ \$47/person
under each, and the incremental QALY differs by only a few hundredths between them — the same
agreement the capacity sweep showed by its precise within-model estimator. The only residual
is directional and second-order: under the most extreme saturation, A's analytic M/M/c wait
is a touch *optimistic* relative to B's exact queue (it admits a few more patients before the
line is truly full), so it nudges the QALY estimate up by a sliver. It is never enough to
change the quadrant — but it is the reason that, when a recommendation sits right on the
SE/SW boundary, you reach for B.
:::

### The tradeoff, stated plainly

So which to use? It depends on the regime, and the table is the guide:

- **Mild contention** (the queue rarely binds): A and B agree to within noise. Prefer **A** —
  it adds the queue with one resource and two registry events, never edits the engine, and
  has none of B's fragile signal-and-clone machinery.
- **Heavy contention** (the queue saturates — exactly the policy-relevant case here, where a
  cheap test floods a fixed capacity): A's analytic wait drifts optimistic. Prefer **B** —
  its queue is the exact emergent FIFO, and when the recommendation sits on the SE/SW
  boundary you want the model that does not approximate the very thing the decision hinges
  on. B is the **defensible** choice for a real recommendation; A is the fast, transparent
  check that tells you whether contention matters at all before you pay for B.

## What the decision looks like

For the Republic of SMDM, the analysis does not hand back a verdict; it hands back the
*shape* of the choice. The field test is genuinely cheaper and genuinely reaches more women —
but only if the confirmatory pathway can absorb what it sends. As modelled, it cannot: the
bottleneck converts reach into waiting, and waiting into progression. The lever that decides
the outcome is therefore not the test at all — it is **capacity**. Adopting the field test
*and* expanding confirmatory throughput could keep it in the southeast; adopting it alone
moves it to the southwest. That coupling — between a screening choice and a downstream
resource — is invisible to a model that treats confirmation as instantaneous or its wait as
fixed, and it is the entire reason to reach for discrete-event simulation here.

## Limitations and honest extensions

This is a deliberately spare, generic model; several real features are omitted, each of
which would deepen (not reverse) the story:

- **False-positive harms are costs only, not health.** A false positive here pays for a test
  and a workup and consumes a slot, but suffers no anxiety, procedure risk, or disutility.
  The field test's heavy false-positive burden would look worse, not better, with those on
  the health axis.
- **No overdiagnosis.** Every detected `S1` case here would have progressed; none is indolent
  disease that screening finds and treats needlessly. Overdiagnosis is a central screening
  harm and would further penalise the higher-coverage test.
- **One bottleneck, not two.** Only confirmation is capacity-constrained; oncology treatment
  is assumed available on demand. Real systems queue there too.
- **Loss-to-follow-up is folded into progression.** Patients leave the queue only by
  progressing, recovering, or dying — not by disengaging after a long wait, which in the
  case study falls hardest on the rural women the expansion is meant to reach. An explicit
  dropout hazard is the natural next event to add.
- **Constant hazards, no age structure; a single lumped advanced state.** Standard
  simplifications for a teaching model; none is load-bearing for the SE→SW result.

The point of the build was never the specific numbers; it was the mechanism — that a finite
downstream resource, modelled endogenously, can move a cost-effectiveness result across the
quadrant boundary — and the two faithful ways to model it.


# Appendix — `simmer` semantics that matter {.appendix}

**Objective:** collect, in one place, the verified `simmer` 4.4.7 facts that the two designs in Part III rest on — the ones that force the shared invariant (never block the patient) and that make Approach A robust and Approach B both powerful and fragile. This appendix is the **reference card** you can return to. Every row was checked empirically against the actual code (`validation/`), and is documented at greater length in [`methodology.md`](methodology.md) §2–3. Nothing here is folklore; where a claim sounds surprising, it is because the obvious reading is wrong.

## The load-bearing facts, one table

The whole document rests on a short list of primitives behaving in a specific, occasionally counter-intuitive way. Read this as the contract: if any one of these were false, the corresponding trap would *not* be a trap, or the corresponding design would *not* hold.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-semantics-table
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Primitive = c(
      "`seize()` on a full resource",
      "`trap()` / `wait()`",
      "`send()`",
      "`renege_if()` / `renege_in()`",
      "`clone()`",
      "`synchronize(wait = ...)`",
      "`rollback(n, times)`",
      "`get_server_count()` / `get_capacity()` / `get_queue_count()` / `get_seized()`"
    ),
    `What it actually does (4.4.7)` = c(
      "**blocks the whole arrival** in the resource's FIFO queue; its hand-rolled event clock freezes",
      "**ignored while the arrival is blocked in `seize()`** — only a renege can pull a queued arrival out",
      "a **global broadcast** to every listener; it is not addressable to one arrival",
      "**fires even while blocked in `seize()`**; `keep_seized` defaults **FALSE** (held resources auto-released on renege)",
      "produces **distinct arrivals with independent seize ledgers** that share attribute *values* only",
      "`wait = FALSE`: the **first** finisher survives and re-enters the enclosing loop. `wait = TRUE`: waits for **all** siblings, last survives. Discarded clones' held resources **leak**",
      "counts **trajectory activity nodes**, not runtime events; `clone`/`synchronize` add nodes and re-inject the survivor",
      "**callable mid-trajectory and inside a `time_to_event` sampler**; they read *live* occupancy of a real resource"
    ),
    `Consequence for us` = c(
      "the core incompatibility — **never block the patient arrival** (the shared invariant of Part III)",
      "a queued patient cannot fire its own competing events; per-patient targeting must be string-encoded and is read only once *unblocked*",
      "per-patient signals are faked by baking the id into the name (B's `acq_<pid>` / `abandon_<pid>`); a single mismatch is silently dropped",
      "the **only** lever that can pull an arrival out of a queue — B's companion uses it to abandon when the patient leaves S1",
      "a pre-clone seize redeemed by both children **double-releases** and aborts the run — so B's companion holds no tally",
      "B relies on `wait = FALSE` so the self-clone survives; `wait = TRUE` **deadlocks** on a parked sibling",
      "if clones are present, integer targets shift — use **tag-named** targets or a `check=` predicate (a runaway otherwise)",
      "this is what makes **Approach A possible**: an endogenous wait with **no blocking** (`years_till_confirm` reads `get_server_count` vs `get_capacity`)"
    ),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = "Verified `simmer` 4.4.7 semantics (methodology.md §2–3). The first four rows defeat the tempting fixes; the last four are what the working designs build on."
)
```

A reader who internalises only this table can reconstruct the rest. The tempting fixes that *don't* work are exactly the ones that assume one of rows 1–6 behaves *intuitively* instead of as written; A and B are exactly the designs that take rows 5–8 at face value and route around rows 1–4.

## Three facts worth restating in prose

A few of these are subtle enough that the one-line table cell undersells them. Each of these three is a place where careful, reasonable code is silently wrong.

::: {.callout-important}
## `send()` is global; a queued arrival is deaf to it anyway

These two facts compound. First, there is **no per-arrival signal channel** in `simmer` — `send("x")` wakes *every* arrival currently in `trap("x")` / `wait()`. The only way to address one patient is to encode the patient id into the signal *string* (`paste0("acq_", pid)`), and a typo or attribute mismatch in that string is dropped without any error. Second, and worse for the naive fix, an arrival that is **blocked inside `seize()` does not process `trap()`/`wait()` at all** — the signal machinery is suspended for the duration of the block. So the one patient you most want to reach (the one stuck in the queue) is precisely the one a broadcast cannot wake. This is why Approach B never lets the *patient* block: only the disposable companion sits in the `seize` queue, and it is reachable via `renege_if`, not `trap`.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Clones carry attribute *values*, not the seize *ledger*

`clone()` is not a deep copy of process state. The children share a snapshot of attribute values, but each maintains its **own, private record of which resources it currently holds**. A resource seized *before* the `clone()` therefore sits in an ambiguous place: each child believes it can release it, but the underlying server count can only be decremented once. The second release underflows the count and `simmer` aborts mid-run (`'<resource>' not previously seized`). Because the offending release happens at an RNG-dependent moment, the crash looks *intermittent* — the most expensive kind of bug to chase. The discipline that follows (and that Approach B obeys): **never seize a shared tally on the patient before cloning, and never let a clone touch the state counters at all.** B's companion touches only the contended `confirm` resource; the patient touches only its tallies. The clone boundary is also a resource boundary, so no ledger is ever redeemed twice.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Live occupancy is readable from inside a `time_to_event` sampler

This is the single permissive fact the whole of Approach A turns on, and it is easy to assume is forbidden. A `time_to_event` function in the event registry is just an R closure evaluated when the engine reschedules; nothing stops it from calling `get_server_count(env, "confirm")` and `get_capacity(env, "confirm")` on a *real* finite resource. So congestion can be read at sampling time and converted directly into a wait — longer when more slots are busy and more patients sit ahead in the FIFO position — with the patient never entering a blocking `seize`. The cap is then enforced *separately*, at fire time, by a guard that performs the real `seize` only when `get_server_count < get_capacity`. The wait is an analytic M/M/c-flavoured approximation (correct mean under saturation); the capacity is exact. Rows 1–2 forbid blocking the patient; row 8 is what lets you avoid it without abandoning a real resource.
:::

## Where each fact is exercised

To close the loop between this reference and the code, the table below points each fact at the specific design decision it underwrites — so a future maintainer touching `model10.R` (A) or `model11.R` (B) knows which invariant they are standing on.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-where-exercised
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Fact = c(
      "blocking `seize()` freezes the clock",
      "`trap()`/`wait()` ignored while blocked; `send()` global",
      "`renege_if` fires from a `seize` queue",
      "live occupancy readable in `time_to_event`",
      "clones have independent seize ledgers",
      "`synchronize(wait = FALSE)` first survives & re-enters",
      "`rollback` counts nodes, not events"
    ),
    `Relied on by` = c(
      "the **shared invariant** — both A and B keep the patient out of every blocking seize",
      "**B**'s per-patient `sig_acq` / `sig_abandon` string-encoded signals (the companion, not the patient, listens)",
      "**B**'s abandonment: leaving S1 sends `abandon_<pid>`; a still-queued companion reneges out",
      "**A**'s `years_till_confirm()` and its fire-time free-slot guard — capacity exact, no blocking",
      "the **avoidance rule**: A uses no clones at all; B's companion touches only `confirm`, never a tally",
      "**B**'s `clone(n = 2, self, companion) |> synchronize(wait = FALSE)` — the self-clone re-enters the loop",
      "**B**'s clone machinery is kept strictly inside the `branch` wrapper so loop targets do not shift"
    ),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = "Each verified fact, mapped to the design decision it underwrites in model10 (A) / model11 (B)."
)
```

The pattern is worth naming. **Approach A's robustness comes from using only the permissive facts** (rows 7–8 of the first table) and the one prohibition that costs nothing (don't block the patient) — it never touches `clone`, `synchronize`, `send`, or `trap`, so none of the fragility in rows 5–6 can reach it. **Approach B is more powerful and more fragile because it uses all eight facts at once**: it accepts the blocking `seize` (row 1) but quarantines it inside a disposable companion, then threads `renege`, `send`/`trap`, `clone`, and `synchronize` together so that every one of their sharp edges (rows 2–6) is pointed away from the patient's state. That is the whole tradeoff of Part IV, reduced to which rows of this table each design chooses to depend on.

## Common random numbers: the design, and its one hard limit

The variance-reduction substrate (`R/crn.R`) deserves its own note, because it has a sharp
boundary that is easy to cross by accident.

**The design.** `simmer` runs every arrival off one global RNG stream, so the textbook CRN
move — `set.seed()` before each arm — desynchronises the instant one arm takes a branch the
other does not. Instead, each patient owns a **private bank** of uniforms, drawn once from a
deterministic per-patient seed, and every stochastic step consumes the bank by inverse-CDF
(`qexp(u, rate)` for `rexp`, `u < p` for `runif`). Because the bank is private and fixed,
two *strategies* hand patient *i* identical draws; patient *i*'s disease is bit-for-bit the
same in both arms until the screening *decision* diverges, so the paired difference is the
decision's effect with the cohort noise differenced away. The helpers `draw_exp()` /
`draw_unif()` fall back to plain `rexp` / `runif` when no bank is armed, which is why Models
1–6 are unchanged to the last digit.

**The hard limit.** CRN aligns two *strategies within one model*. It **cannot** align two
*different models* — Approach A and Approach B inject different confirm-handling events into
the loop, so the reactive resample consumes each patient's disease bank at a different
*cadence*, and the same seed yields different draws. A shared-seed A-vs-B comparison
therefore measures that cadence artifact, not the models; we even see A ≠ B under a
*null-effect* run, where the queue is inert. So A-vs-B agreement must be established by
**independent replication** (Part IV), not by CRN — a subtle but load-bearing distinction
when the two models are being compared head-to-head.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A practical gotcha in the banks
The per-patient seed is `CRN$seed + patient_index`, so two runs whose seeds differ by less
than the cohort size draw **overlapping** banks — their "independent" cohorts are nearly
identical. For genuinely independent replications (e.g. the variance demo in Model 8, or the
A-vs-B harness), space the run seeds widely (`seed * 123457`), not by consecutive integers.
:::
